subQuestions.questionText: The pressure cell labelled L over the interior is best described as a … (Refer to Figure 1.1 — South African synoptic weather map in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B continental thermal low (1 mark)
Interior heating in summer produces a low-pressure cell over the plateau.

subQuestions.questionText: The two anticyclones flanking South Africa in Figure 1.1 are the … (Refer to Figure 1.1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: B South Atlantic High and South Indian High (1 mark)

options.B: South Atlantic High and South Indian High
options.D: South Pacific High and South Indian High

subQuestions.questionText: Air movement around the Continental Thermal Low (in the Southern Hemisphere) is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C anticlockwise and convergent (1 mark)
Low-pressure cell in the Southern Hemisphere has anticlockwise circulation with surface convergence.

subQuestions.questionText: The isobars on the map are drawn at intervals of …
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: B 4 hPa (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: At Station A (Cape Town area), the wind is blowing from the …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D south-west (1 mark)
The wind shaft points to the SW; wind is named for the direction it blows FROM.

subQuestions.questionText: Cloud cover at Station A is best described as …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D completely overcast (1 mark)
A filled circle on the station model represents fully overcast skies.

subQuestions.questionText: The wind speed shown at Station A is approximately …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C 25 knots (1 mark)
Two full barbs + one half barb = 10 + 10 + 5 = 25 knots.

subQuestions.questionText: The cold front shown south of South Africa is moving in a …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A north-easterly direction (1 mark)
The triangles on the cold front symbol point in the direction of movement (NE).

subQuestions.questionText: Match the feature 'Pollution dome' with the correct letter (P, Q, R, S or T) labelled on Figure 1.2 — Cross-section of a valley showing night-time microclimate features. (Refer to Figure 1.2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: Q (1 mark)
A pollution dome forms over the valley floor at night when cold-air pooling and the inversion layer trap pollutants.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the feature 'Frost pocket' with the correct letter (P, Q, R, S or T) labelled on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: R (1 mark)
The frost pocket is the lowest part of the valley floor where the coldest, densest air collects.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the feature 'Katabatic (downslope) wind' with the correct letter (P, Q, R, S or T) labelled on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: P (1 mark)
Katabatic winds drain cold dense air down the slopes at night.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the feature 'Temperature inversion layer' with the correct letter (P, Q, R, S or T) labelled on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: T (1 mark)
The inversion layer is the boundary where warmer air sits above the cold pooled air on the valley floor.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the feature 'Thermal belt' with the correct letter (P, Q, R, S or T) labelled on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: S (1 mark)
The thermal belt is the warm zone on the upper slope above the inversion layer.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the feature 'Air that has cooled by terrestrial radiation' with the correct letter (P, Q, R, S or T) labelled on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: R (1 mark)
This cold-air pool on the valley floor results from terrestrial radiation losses overnight.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the feature 'The warmest zone on the slope at night' with the correct letter (P, Q, R, S or T) labelled on Figure 1.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: S (1 mark)
The thermal belt on the upper slope is the warmest zone at night because it lies above the inversion layer.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the type of low-pressure system labelled L in Figure 1.3. (Refer to Figure 1.3 — Cold front from a mid-latitude cyclone advancing over the Western Cape in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Mid-latitude cyclone / temperate cyclone / extratropical cyclone (any one) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Name the front that is currently making landfall over the Western Cape. (Refer to Figure 1.3 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Cold front (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: State the direction in which this front is advancing. (Refer to Figure 1.3 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: North-east / north-easterly / NE (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the wind change a coastal observer at Cape Town would experience as the front passes overhead. Refer to BOTH wind direction and the technical name for this change in the Southern Hemisphere.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Wind shifts from NW (ahead of the front, in the warm sector) to SW (behind the front, in the cool air) (1 mark)
Mark 2: In the Southern Hemisphere this anti-clockwise change is called backing (NOT veering) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain why the rainfall probability decreases sharply from Cape Town (85%) to Johannesburg (10%) as shown on the map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Cape Town and George lie immediately on/behind the cold front, so the steep frontal uplift and unstable cold air produce heavy rain (~85% / 70% probability) (1 mark)
Mark 2: By the time the front reaches the interior its moisture has largely been precipitated out and the front has weakened, so probability drops to ~10% at Johannesburg (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: In a paragraph of 8–10 lines, discuss the impact of this cold front on tourism in the Western Cape. In your answer, refer to BOTH negative and positive effects, and use evidence from Figure 1.3. (Use Level 1–4 paragraph rubric.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Level 1–4 holistic rubric:
• Level 4 (7–8 marks): Clear, well-supported argument; both relevant geographical evidence AND own knowledge integrated; counter-perspective acknowledged; conclusion answers the question directly. Sophisticated, accurate use of geographical terminology.
• Level 3 (5–6 marks): Argument present; relevant evidence referenced; some own knowledge; limited counter-perspective. Mostly accurate use of terminology.
• Level 2 (3–4 marks): Some evidence used; limited own knowledge; argument weak or implied. Basic terminology, occasional inaccuracies.
• Level 1 (1–2 marks): Mostly descriptive; little or no relevant evidence; no clear argument. Limited or incorrect terminology.

Suggested content for full marks:

Negative impacts:
• Strong frontal winds force closure of Table Mountain Cableway and ferries to Robben Island, stranding visitors.
• Heavy rain reduces visibility for whale-watching at Hermanus and game-viewing at private reserves.
• Wet, cold conditions deter beach tourism along the Atlantic Seaboard and Camps Bay.
• Flight delays and diversions at Cape Town International, disrupting arrivals.
• Vineyards and wine-tour bookings affected by saturated roads and damaged vines.

Positive / counter-balancing impacts:
• Front-fed rain replenishes Western Cape dam levels (Theewaterskloof, etc.) — long-term benefit for tourism dependent on water supply.
• Snowfall on Matroosberg/Cederberg attracts winter tourists.
• Western Cape winter rainfall is expected — operators have adapted (indoor activities, heated venues, winter discounts).

Strong responses use at least one piece of evidence from Figure 1.3 (e.g., 85% rain probability at Cape Town) AND own knowledge of WC tourism products. The conclusion must directly state whether the front is mostly negative or mostly negative-but-mitigated for WC tourism.

subQuestions.questionText: Name the body of water in which this tropical cyclone formed. (Refer to Figure 1.4 — Tropical cyclone path map and cross-section in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Mozambique Channel (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: On which date does the cyclone make landfall along the African coast? (Refer to Figure 1.4 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: 27 February (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO conditions necessary for the formation of a tropical cyclone over the ocean.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each, max 2):
• Sea-surface temperature ≥ 27 °C to a depth of ~50 m
• Latitude between 5°–30° (Coriolis effect strong enough to spin the system)
• Low vertical wind shear in the troposphere
• High humidity in the lower-middle troposphere
• Pre-existing low-level disturbance / convergence

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the part of the cyclone labelled X on the cross-section. (Refer to Figure 1.4 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: The eye of the cyclone (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Describe the air movement at point X AND explain how it produces calm, clear weather there.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Air at X is descending / subsiding (1 mark)
Mark 2: As it descends it warms adiabatically, evaporating any cloud (1 mark)
Mark 3: This produces calm, clear, almost cloud-free conditions in the eye (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the part of the cyclone labelled Y. (Refer to Figure 1.4 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: The eyewall (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Describe what is happening to air at Y, and explain why this causes the most violent weather of the entire system.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Air at Y is rising rapidly (strong updrafts) (1 mark)
Mark 2: Latent heat release as moisture condenses fuels further uplift, producing the deepest cumulonimbus (Cb) cloud and most intense rain in the system (1 mark)
Mark 3: Strongest winds and heaviest rainfall therefore occur in the eyewall — this is why it produces the most violent weather (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: In which hemisphere did this cyclone form? Justify your answer using ONE piece of evidence from the path map.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Southern Hemisphere (1 mark)
Mark 2: Justification: spiral of the cyclone curls clockwise as drawn (path moves SW from the equatorial side; SH cyclones rotate clockwise) — accept any single valid piece of map evidence (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest ONE strategy that the Mozambican government could implement BEFORE landfall to reduce loss of life.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE (1 mark):
• Issue early-warning broadcasts via radio/TV/SMS
• Evacuate low-lying coastal communities to inland shelters
• Pre-position food, water and medical supplies in safe zones
• Reinforce or board up windows of public buildings
• Stop fishing fleets from going to sea

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term line thunderstorm. (Refer to Figure 1.5 — Cross-section along a line (squall) thunderstorm over the highveld interior in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: A line thunderstorm is a row / line of cumulonimbus cells (1 mark)
Mark 2: Produced along a convergence (squall) line at the surface, often along an advancing cold front or a moisture front (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the cloud type that forms each cell shown in Figure 1.5.
subQuestions.memoText: Cumulonimbus (Cb) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: State the time of day and time of year (season) when line thunderstorms most commonly occur over the South African highveld.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Late afternoon / early evening (1 mark)
Mark 2: Late spring to summer (October–March / wet season) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Name the feature labelled X at the top of the cell. (Refer to Figure 1.5 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText: Anvil / anvil top of cirrus (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain what causes the flat, spreading shape of the feature at X.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Updrafts rise to the tropopause where stable air halts further uplift (1 mark)
Mark 2: The cloud spreads horizontally as ice crystals — producing the flat anvil shape and characteristic cirrus extension (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Describe what is happening to the air at Y AND explain how it gives rise to lightning.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Air at Y is rising strongly (updraft) (1 mark)
Mark 2: Within the cell, ice crystals and water droplets collide, separating positive and negative charges (1 mark)
Mark 3: When the potential difference between cloud and ground becomes large enough, the air ionises and lightning discharges (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Describe what is happening to the air at Z AND explain how it produces a sudden drop in surface temperature ahead of the storm.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Air at Z is descending (downdraft) and is cooled by the evaporation of raindrops (1 mark)
Mark 2: When this cold downdraft hits the surface, it spreads out as a gust front, causing a sudden drop in temperature and a sharp wind change ahead of the storm (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest TWO precautions a farmer should take before a line thunderstorm reaches their land.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Move livestock and machinery into shelter / barns
• Cover seedlings; do not work in tall fields during the storm
• Switch off and unplug electric pumps and irrigation controllers (lightning surge)
• Check and clear stormwater drainage channels
• Stop all field work and seek shelter in a hard-roofed building

subQuestions.questionText: Feature 1 on the drainage basin sketch is the … (Refer to Figure 2.1 — Drainage basin features 1–6 and drainage patterns P, Q, R, S in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C source (1 mark)
The upland point where the river begins.

subQuestions.questionText: Feature 4 is the … (Refer to Figure 2.1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D watershed (1 mark)
A point on the basin's high-lying boundary.

subQuestions.questionText: Drainage Pattern P develops most readily on … (Refer to Figure 2.1 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A uniformly soft, gently sloping rock (1 mark)
This favours the dendritic / tree-like pattern.

options.B: steeply tilted strata of varying hardness

subQuestions.questionText: Drainage Pattern Q is best described as a …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B trellis pattern (1 mark)
Parallel mains crossed by perpendicular tributaries.

subQuestions.questionText: The pattern that develops on a dome or volcanic peak is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C R (1 mark)
Radial pattern — streams flow outwards from a central peak / dome.

subQuestions.questionText: Right-angled bends typical of jointed bedrock are most clearly shown by …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D S (1 mark)
Rectangular pattern — right-angled bends along joints / faults.

subQuestions.questionText: Using Strahler's method, the order of the main river just before its mouth (feature 2) is …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C third order (1 mark)
Strahler: when two same-order streams meet, the order increases.

subQuestions.questionText: The high-lying line shown by the dashed boundary is called the …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B watershed (1 mark)
The basin boundary.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'A river that has reached equilibrium between erosion and deposition' to the correct letter from Figure 2.2 — River Profiles. Choices: graded curve · ungraded curve · X · Y · Z · sea level · lower course. (Refer to Figure 2.2 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: graded curve (1 mark)
A graded longitudinal profile shows equilibrium between erosion and deposition.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'A profile that contains a knickpoint and waterfall' to the correct letter from Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: ungraded curve (1 mark)
The ungraded longitudinal profile contains breaks of slope (knickpoints) and waterfalls.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Cross profile typical of the upper course (steep gradient, vertical erosion)' to the correct letter from Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: X (1 mark)
The V-shaped cross profile of the upper course.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Cross profile typical of the middle course (lateral erosion begins)' to the correct letter from Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: Y (1 mark)
The wider U-shaped / box cross profile of the middle course.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Cross profile typical of the lower course (broad floodplain)' to the correct letter from Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: Z (1 mark)
The flat-floored cross profile of the lower course with a wide floodplain.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'The permanent base level of erosion' to the correct letter from Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: sea level (1 mark)
Sea level is the permanent base level — rivers cannot erode below it.

subQuestions.questionText: Match the description 'Where deposition dominates over erosion' to the correct letter from Figure 2.2.
subQuestions.memoText:
Answer: lower course / Z (1 mark)
Deposition dominates in the lower course where the gradient is gentle and discharge slows.

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term meander. (Refer to Figure 2.3 — Meander plan view and cross-section in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: A meander is a pronounced bend / loop in a river's course (1 mark)
Mark 2: Produced as the channel shifts laterally on its floodplain (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the feature labelled O on the plan view AND state the dominant fluvial process operating there. (Refer to Figure 2.3 in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Feature O = the outer / undercut bank (1 mark)
Mark 2: Dominant process: erosion (lateral / undercut erosion by faster, deeper flow) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the feature labelled I on the plan view AND state the dominant fluvial process operating there.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Feature I = the inner / slip-off bank (point bar) (1 mark)
Mark 2: Dominant process: deposition by slower water on the inside of the bend (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the cross-section A–A'. Describe TWO ways in which the channel cross-section is asymmetrical.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of (1 mark each):
• The outer (right) bank is steep and almost vertical, while the inner (left) bank slopes gently down to the channel.
• The deepest part of the channel sits against the outer bank, not in the centre.
• A point-bar deposit (sand/gravel) builds out from the inner bank.

subQuestions.questionText: Account for the location of the deepest part of the channel (the thalweg) close to the outer bank.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: As water rounds the bend, centrifugal force pushes the fastest, most erosive flow to the outside of the meander (1 mark)
Mark 2: This concentrated, high-energy flow erodes the outer bank vertically and laterally, creating the deepest channel position (thalweg) there (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the small water body to the left of the active river on the plan view AND explain how it forms.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: It is an oxbow lake (1 mark)
Mark 2: Erosion at the outer bank narrows the meander neck until the river breaks through (usually during a flood) (1 mark)
Mark 3: The old loop is cut off and gradually silts up, leaving a crescent-shaped lake (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest TWO reasons why farmers value the inner-bank land of meandering rivers.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Soils on the inner bank are made up of fertile alluvium / silt / clay deposits.
• Gentle slope — easy to plough and irrigate.
• Closer to water for irrigation and livestock.
• Less risk of bank collapse than on the steep outer bank.

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term river rejuvenation. (Refer to Figure 2.4 — Oblique sketch of a rejuvenated river system in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: River rejuvenation is the renewal / restoration of a river's erosive ability (1 mark)
Mark 2: After a fall in base level (or uplift of the land), so that the river starts to incise / deepen its valley once more (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify TWO causes of river rejuvenation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Tectonic uplift of the land (relative drop in base level)
• Fall in sea level (eustatic change)
• Increase in discharge (e.g., capture of an upstream river or higher rainfall)
• Reduction in sediment load (e.g., damming upstream)
• Lowering of a temporary base level (e.g., dam wall destroyed)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the feature labelled 1 on Figure 2.4 AND describe how it forms during rejuvenation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Feature 1 = a river terrace (1 mark)
Mark 2: It is a remnant of the old, higher floodplain (1 mark)
Mark 3: Left perched above the new, deeper valley after the river rejuvenated and incised (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the feature labelled 2 AND explain why it migrates upstream over time.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Feature 2 = the knickpoint / waterfall (1 mark)
Mark 2: It marks the boundary between the new (lower) profile downstream and the old profile still being adjusted upstream (1 mark)
Mark 3: Headward erosion at the base of the falls undercuts the rock face, so the knickpoint retreats upstream over time (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Compare the position of feature 4 with feature 5 AND explain what this difference tells us about base-level change.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Feature 4 (new base level) lies well below feature 5 (old base level) (1 mark)
Mark 2: This vertical difference shows that base level has fallen (relative drop in sea level OR tectonic uplift) (1 mark)
Mark 3: The fall has rejuvenated the river — it is now eroding downwards toward the new, lower base level (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Suggest ONE way in which the formation of feature 3 (incised meander) influences settlement patterns along the river.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid suggestion (1 mark) + reason (1 mark):
• Settlements concentrate on the flat terraces rather than in the steep incised valley — terraces are level, well-drained and above flood level.
• Bridges and roads must climb out of the deep gorge — affects routes / costs.
• Hydropower potential at the knickpoint encourages dam-side settlement.

subQuestions.questionText: Quote ONE phrase from the extract that shows the Vaal River pollution is caused by MORE than one source. (Refer to the extract 'VAAL RIVER UNDER PRESSURE — Adapted news report, 2025' in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE phrase that names multiple sources (1 mark), e.g.:
• 'Industrial discharge from mines and factories upstream of the Vaal Dam has added high concentrations of heavy metals'
• 'Untreated sewage from failing wastewater treatment works ... continues to flow directly into the river'
(Source: extract.)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify TWO different sources of pollution mentioned in the extract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO of (1 mark each):
• Untreated sewage from failing wastewater works (Sedibeng / Emfuleni)
• Industrial discharge / heavy metals from mines and factories
• Faecal pollution from informal settlements without proper sanitation

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how untreated sewage entering the river affects aquatic life.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Sewage adds excess nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) — promotes algal blooms (1 mark)
Mark 2: Decomposition of sewage and dead algae lowers dissolved-oxygen levels (eutrophication), killing fish and invertebrates (fish kills) (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: State TWO economic activities along the Vaal that are directly damaged by the pollution described in the extract.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO (1 mark each):
• Tourism / recreation operators (bookings collapsed)
• Irrigation farming (crops rejected by export markets)
• Drinking-water supply for downstream communities
• Fishing

subQuestions.questionText: In a paragraph of 8–10 lines, discuss the strategies that government, business and communities can implement to manage and rehabilitate the Vaal River catchment. Use evidence from the extract AND your own knowledge. (Use Level 1–4 paragraph rubric.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Apply the Level 1–4 holistic rubric:
• Level 4 (7–8 marks): Clear, well-supported argument; both relevant geographical evidence AND own knowledge integrated; counter-perspective acknowledged; conclusion answers the question directly. Sophisticated, accurate use of geographical terminology.
• Level 3 (5–6 marks): Argument present; relevant evidence referenced; some own knowledge; limited counter-perspective. Mostly accurate use of terminology.
• Level 2 (3–4 marks): Some evidence used; limited own knowledge; argument weak or implied. Basic terminology, occasional inaccuracies.
• Level 1 (1–2 marks): Mostly descriptive; little or no relevant evidence; no clear argument. Limited or incorrect terminology.

Suggested content for full marks:

Government / regulatory:
• Enforce existing legislation — National Water Act (1998) and National Environmental Management Act (NEMA): polluter-pays principle, fines, prosecution of municipalities and industries that discharge untreated effluent.
• Fix sewage infrastructure — repair / upgrade failing wastewater treatment works in Emfuleni and Sedibeng; invest in pump stations.
• Regular water-quality monitoring at multiple sites; publish results so communities can hold polluters accountable.

Industry / mining:
• Treat industrial effluent before discharge; require zero-effluent licences.
• Recycle mine water — Acid Mine Drainage (AMD) treatment plants.

Community / ecological:
• Plant indigenous riparian vegetation (reeds, sedges) — natural filter for nutrients and sediment, stabilises banks.
• Build artificial wetlands as natural water-quality filters.
• Educate communities about safe sanitation and the importance of catchment health (school programmes, river-keeper / clean-up days).

Strong responses use the extract evidence ('no single department can solve this on its own') AND own knowledge to argue that integrated catchment management (national + provincial + municipal + community) is essential. The conclusion must directly state which strategy mix the candidate sees as most effective and why.
